forecaster.notes: No vote counts or results from 2026-11-03 were seen. The harness was in plan mode, so only read-only web research was done. One WebFetch of the Census release PDF came back unreadable, and the tool saved a local copy that I did not open. The Census data-center baseline therefore comes from a secondary report I could not check against Census tables. Early-vote figures (about 4.5M in the first 7 days; 23.4% of registered voters by Oct 25 vs 24.3% at the same point in 2018) informed the turnout forecast.

research_summary: Final independent polls had Abbott ahead of Hinojosa by about 3–4 points: TPOR 51–48, TSU 50–47, UH Hobby 49–46, ActiVote 52.1–47.9. The only poll with her ahead, GBAO 47–45, was released by her campaign. Talarico runs about 2–3 points ahead of Hinojosa in margin, from a tie to +5 over Paxton. Early voting tracked just below 2018's pace as a share of registered voters, on a much larger registered-voter base. On data centers: in June 2026 Abbott asked the 2027 Legislature to end the data center sales tax exemption, make data centers pay for their own grid connections and require closed-loop water systems. His Aug. 3 directive paused ERCOT approvals for data centers of 75 MW or more until a verification audit is done; the reports are due Dec. 10, 2026, and site-readiness checks can run to April 2027. Hinojosa wants the exemption repealed, a moratorium and a special session. ERCOT's Approval to Energize total stayed flat in 2026: 8,786 MW in Jan, 9,062 MW in May, 8,926 MW in June. The Comptroller lists 61 projects with 2026 effective dates as of Nov. 3, against 49 in 2025. A secondary analysis puts Census private data-center construction at an $84.95B annual rate in Aug 2026, against about $50.7B in April. New York's legislative moratorium bill is still waiting on Hochul, who has until year-end, and her one-year executive-order moratorium has been in effect since July. Maine's moratorium was vetoed.

dem_share.reasoning: Independent late polls put Abbott ahead by about 3–4 points, which is about 48.2% of the two-party vote for Hinojosa. Texas polls have historically understated Republicans slightly. A midterm under a Republican president favors Democrats and offsets that. The median is 48.0% with a standard deviation of about 2.6 and fat tails, which gives Hinojosa about a 22% chance of winning.

turnout.reasoning: In 2018, the two candidates got about 8.2M votes combined, and in 2022 about 7.8M. Registration has grown to about 18.6M or more. The 2026 early vote ran just behind 2018's rate and ahead of 2022's. If turnout is about 51–53% of registered voters, the total is about 9.5–9.8M ballots, and about 9.4M of those go to the two major candidates.

senate_dem_share.reasoning: Talarico has polled about 5–7 points of margin ahead of Hinojosa, so roughly 2.5–3 points of two-party share. Paxton is a weaker nominee than Abbott. Ticket splitting in Texas is limited, so the two races move together. Talarico's edge is about 2.7 points in the low cells and shrinks to about 1.8 at 56%, where the environment rather than candidate quality drives both results.

ercot_pause_lifted.reasoning: The pause holds until the verification and audit reports, due Dec. 10, 2026, are done. Site-readiness checks can run to April 2027. If Abbott wins, verified loads are likely approved again in the first half of 2027, which is what the audit was set up to do. A Governor Hinojosa wants a moratorium and could keep the pause going. The PUC commissioners are Abbott appointees, though, and the legislature could force a resumption, so the chance stays at about 40–50%.

special_session_data_centers.reasoning: Texas has held special sessions after most recent regular sessions. Abbott has put data centers on the 2027 regular-session agenda and is unlikely to call a special session for them unless the regular session fails. Hinojosa has made a data center special session a campaign promise. As governor she would face a Republican legislature and would likely call one, or add data centers to one, if the regular session fell short.

tax_exemption_cut.reasoning: Both candidates want to end or narrow the exemption, which costs about $3.2–3.3B per biennium, and Abbott formally recommended this to the 2027 Legislature. Industry lobbying and the incentive-friendly instincts of Texas Republicans are the main obstacles. Any narrowing counts, such as closing the exemption to new certifications or removing electricity from it, which makes passage more likely. A Hinojosa win changes little, because the Republican legislature decides what passes.

restriction_law.reasoning: Abbott's 2027 package includes making data centers pay for their own grid connections and requiring closed-loop water systems, and either would count. Public backlash is broad and bipartisan, so some qualifying limit on water, grid costs or siting is likely to pass. Industry can still water bills down to reporting-only versions that don't count. Higher Democratic shares bring a somewhat more restriction-minded legislature and a governor who would sign.

baseline.source: ERCOT Monthly Operational Overview June 2026 (https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/07/17/ERCOT-Monthly-Operational-Overview-June-2026.pdf); 9,042 MW on 2026-03-13 in the March TAC Report

ercot_approved_mw_2027.reasoning: Approvals stayed flat at about 9 GW through 2026, and the pause has blocked data centers since August. ERCOT expected about 3.9 GW to energize in Q4 2026, and that backlog is likely to clear once approvals resume, with Batch Zero allocations adding more. Non-data-center loads keep getting approved meanwhile. Hinojosa cells allow for a longer pause or tighter rules, so their medians are lower.

ercot_approved_mw_2028.reasoning: Batch Zero has 66 GW of base load allocated across 2027–2030. Actual energization is limited by generation, transmission, turbines and the rules that come out of the 2027 session, so I expect about 5–7 GW a year once approvals restart. If Hinojosa wins, her administration and stricter rules slow things down somewhat.

baseline.source: Texas Comptroller data center lists (https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/data-centers/data-center-lists.php): 13 qualifying data centers + 48 large data center projects with 2026 effective dates; 49 with 2025 dates

comptroller_new_projects_2027.reasoning: Registrations are running at about 73 a year in 2026, up from 49 in 2025. If the exemption is likely to close to new certifications, projects may rush to register before the cutoff, which pushes the count up. A cutoff early in 2027 would push it down. A Hinojosa administration and the grid uncertainty around it lower the medians a little.

baseline.source: Secondary analysis of Census Construction Spending (https://www.neoteo.com/en/us-data-center-construction-hit-a-reported-record-annual-pace-in-august); not verified against Census tables; April 2026 SAAR about $50.7B

us_dc_spending_2027.reasoning: The Census data-center series grew from about $31B in 2024 to $41–45B in 2025, and 2026 is running at roughly a $50–85B annual rate. Hyperscaler capex plans point to further growth in 2027. The risks are an AI capex pullback and Census revisions. Texas is a big share but the outcome there moves the national total only slightly, mostly through projects shifting to other states.

baseline.source: Secondary analysis of Census Construction Spending (https://www.neoteo.com/en/us-data-center-construction-hit-a-reported-record-annual-pace-in-august); not verified against Census tables

us_dc_spending_2028.reasoning: Growth likely continues but slows, and the spread is wider because the AI investment cycle could turn by 2028 and power limits restrict building. Texas policy has only a small effect on the national total.

other_state_moratorium.reasoning: New York's legislature passed a statewide moratorium that Hochul must sign or veto by year-end. She has made her own executive-order pause a campaign theme, so signing after Nov. 4 is roughly a coin flip, and a chapter amendment is possible. Her one-year order expires in July 2027 and could be renewed. Moratorium bills in 14 or more other states in 2027 add further chances. A Texas Democratic wave slightly raises the odds of anti-data-center momentum nationally.
